title: Designing a Music Streaming Service: Catalog, Chunked Delivery, and Offline Playback
lesson:
A music streaming service has two very different halves: a catalog (artists, albums, tracks, playlists, search) and a delivery path that gets audio bytes to a player with no audible gaps. The catalog is metadata-heavy and read-dominated, so it is stored in a database with aggressive caching and a search index, while the audio itself lives in object storage and is served through a CDN.

Each track is encoded ahead of time into several bitrates and formats, so the client can pick one based on network conditions and user settings. Audio is split into short segments or byte ranges, and the player requests them sequentially, buffering a few seconds ahead. Because the audio is immutable once published, it caches extremely well at CDN edges, and popular tracks follow a heavy-tailed distribution: a small share of tracks account for most plays, so a high edge hit ratio is realistic. Players can also prefetch the start of the next track in a queue so transitions feel instant.

Offline playback works by downloading encrypted segments to the device along with a licence that has an expiry. The app must periodically reconnect to confirm the subscription is still valid, otherwise the licence lapses. Encryption is about honouring licensing agreements with rights holders, and the keys are tied to the account and device rather than the file.

Play events drive both royalties and recommendations. A play is usually counted only after a minimum listening threshold, and events are sent to a log such as a partitioned queue, then aggregated in batch or stream jobs. Royalty accuracy matters, so events carry unique IDs and consumers deduplicate them. Playback position and queue state are synced across devices through a small per-user state store, with the most recent write winning for simple fields, so a user can pause on a phone and resume on a laptop.

questions.prompt: Why does audio content cache so well at CDN edges?
options: It is immutable once published and popularity is heavily skewed toward a few tracks
It is small enough to fit in browser memory
CDNs transcode it on the fly
questions.explanation: Immutable objects never need invalidation and skewed popularity gives a high hit ratio.

questions.prompt: Encoding each track into multiple bitrates ahead of time lets the client choose a quality that matches its network conditions.
questions.explanation: Pre-encoded variants avoid on-demand transcoding and enable adaptive quality selection.

questions.prompt: Offline downloads are playable only while an unexpired ____ is held on the device.
questions.explanation: The expiring licence forces periodic reconnection so lapsed subscriptions lose offline access.

questions.prompt: Order the flow of a play event used for royalties, earliest first.
items: Events are deduplicated by unique ID and aggregated
The listener passes the minimum listening threshold
The client sends a play event to an event log
Royalty and recommendation jobs consume the aggregates
questions.explanation: A play only counts after the threshold, is logged, deduplicated and aggregated, then consumed downstream.

questions.prompt: Why do play events carry unique IDs?
options: So consumers can deduplicate retries and keep royalty counts accurate
So the CDN can cache them
questions.explanation: Client retries and at-least-once delivery cause duplicates, which would otherwise inflate royalty payments.
